result.summary: Apollo, enchanted by Hermes' lyre, offers friendship and a bargain. Hermes gives him the lyre in exchange for the herds, and the two return to Olympus reconciled. They swear oaths of loyalty, and Apollo gives Hermes a golden staff but refuses to share the prophecy that belongs to Zeus.

scenes.title: Apollo and Hermes talk of the lyre
scenes.summary: Apollo praises the music and promises Hermes renown. Hermes offers him the lyre and asks only to tend the cattle.
scenes.stakes: Apollo wants his stolen cattle settled peacefully; Hermes wants to escape punishment and gain honour.

scenes.title: Exchange of lyre and whip
scenes.summary: Apollo takes the lyre and makes Hermes keeper of herds. They return to Olympus, Zeus reconciles them, and Apollo asks for an oath.
scenes.stakes: Apollo fears the thief may steal his lyre and bow; Hermes' friendship is at stake.

scenes.title: Oaths and Apollo's gifts
scenes.summary: Hermes swears not to steal from Apollo, who swears friendship and gives a golden staff. He refuses to share Zeus's prophecy and describes how omens work.
scenes.stakes: Hermes seeks prophecy but is refused; those who misuse prophecy will fail.

alias_notes.explanation: An epithet of Apollo, as is Far-shooter.

notable_quotes.reason: Apollo states that prophecy of Zeus's mind is forbidden even to the gods.

analysis.text: The hymn resolves the quarrel through exchange: music and cattle trade hands, showing Hermes' cleverness turned into lasting friendship and defined spheres of divine honour.
The passage explains the origins of cattle herding, Hermes' role in barter, and Greek bird omens as aetiology of cult practice.

legacy.text: Hermes' golden staff, the kerykeion, became the caduceus, a symbol still used for commerce and medicine.

fun_facts.text: The hymn says Apollo's oracle works through omens, reflecting the importance of divination at Delphi.

language_notes.text: "Worth fifty cows" refers to the stolen cattle; Apollo says the song alone repays the theft, so the quarrel can end.
"Feats of skill" translates the idea of clever crafts or contrivances; Apollo means no other musical art has ever impressed him as this does.
The cornel-wood shaft is Apollo's staff or spear; swearing by it makes his promise a solemn oath.
"Far-worker" is a standard epithet of Apollo, the archer god who strikes from afar.
Apollo was the god of prophecy, learning Zeus's will and passing it on through oracles such as Delphi.
Hermes offers to graze cattle, taking the herdsman's role, and describes the herds' increase as a blessing.
The 'whip' is the herdsman's goad or lash, the emblem of the office Apollo now hands over: tending cattle.
The 'key' is the plectrum, a small pick used to strike the lyre's strings.
'Deeds of barter' means exchanges and trade between men. 'Form' is a misprint for 'from'.
The oath by the water of Styx, a river of the underworld, was the gods' most binding oath. Nodding the head was also a sign of solemn assent.
'Scatheless' means unharmed; the staff protects Hermes while he carries out tasks.
'Sooth-saying' is prophecy or divination; 'sooth' means truth.
Birds' calls and flight were read as omens. Apollo promises that those who read them rightly will be guided by him truthfully.

context_notes.text: Maia is the mother of Hermes; Zeus is his father. Apollo uses the matronymic to address him respectfully.
The Muses were goddesses of song and arts, and Apollo was their leader and patron of music.
Hermes was a god of herds and shepherds, so tending cattle suits him.
Apollo, son of Leto, is the god of music and prophecy. He is called 'far-working' because he shoots arrows from afar.
The pipes, a reed instrument often called the syrinx or panpipes, are later associated with herdsmen and with Hermes' pastoral role.
Hermes is the god of travellers, commerce and thieves. This explains why Apollo, whose cattle he stole, worries about his thieving.
An eagle was Zeus' sacred bird, and its appearance was a sign of his approval of the oath.

literary_notes.text: Apollo's string of teasing titles for Hermes mixes praise and reproach, matching the mood of grudging reconciliation.
Apollo's rapid questions show his amazement and his eagerness to understand the new instrument.
Hermes' "artful words" are called honest, yet he flatters Apollo to turn the dispute to his advantage.
The lyre is given a will: it teaches the wise, abhors drudgery, and chatters foolishness at the ignorant.
The sound is described as awesome and sweet. This shows the lyre's power and the god's skill.
The phrase 'even as he does now' speaks from the poet's present. It ties the myth to the continuing friendship of the gods.
Apollo presents himself as bound by duty and sworn secrecy, which shows his loyalty to Zeus and his guarded authority over prophecy.
Apollo says he will still take the gifts of those who ignore him, so the offerings are made to no purpose while the god gains.
